question: Why is microbiology considered a foundational pillar in nursing practice?

options.A: It helps nurses understand how diseases spread and how to manage infections
options.B: It replaces the need for pharmacology and anatomy
options.C: It is only useful for laboratory scientists working in research
options.D: It guarantees that patients will never contract a hospital infection

explanation: Microbiology helps nurses understand microorganisms, disease spread, and infection management, forming the basis for safe bedside care. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is another term for hospital-acquired infections mentioned in the text?
explanation: Hospital-acquired infections are also referred to as nosocomial infections in clinical practice. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: How many links make up the complete chain of infection?
explanation: The chain of infection consists of six distinct links: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of interventions like hand hygiene and PPE in nursing?

options.A: To interrupt transmission and break the chain of infection
options.B: To increase the susceptibility of the host
options.C: To create new reservoirs for pathogens
options.D: To speed up the metabolism of infectious agents

explanation: Practical strategies like hand hygiene and personal protective equipment are used to interrupt transmission and break the chain of infection. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which type of asepsis aims to eliminate all microorganisms, both pathogenic and non-pathogenic?
explanation: Surgical asepsis, or sterile technique, eliminates all microorganisms from an object or area, unlike medical asepsis which only reduces their numbers. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h3)

question: During which procedure is surgical asepsis strictly required?
explanation: Invasive procedures like inserting an indwelling urinary catheter require strict surgical asepsis to prevent introducing pathogens into sterile body cavities. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is a primary driver of antimicrobial resistance (AMR)?

options.A: Completing a full course of prescribed antibiotics
options.B: The misuse and overuse of antimicrobial medications
options.C: Strict adherence to infection control protocols
options.D: Obtaining wound cultures before starting treatment

explanation: Misuse and overuse of antibiotics, such as incomplete courses or self-medication, are primary drivers of antimicrobial resistance. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is a key responsibility of the nurse in antimicrobial stewardship?

options.A: Prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics for viral infections
options.B: Educating patients to stop taking drugs when they feel better
options.C: Ensuring cultures are obtained before starting therapy and educating patients

explanation: Nurses support stewardship by ensuring cultures are collected prior to treatment and educating patients on completing their full medication course. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h4)

question: When should diagnostic specimens for culture ideally be collected?

options.A: After the full course of antibiotics is finished
options.C: Three days after starting antibiotic treatment
options.D: Whenever it is most convenient for the laboratory

explanation: Specimens should be collected before starting antimicrobial therapy to prevent antibiotics from suppressing growth and causing false-negative results. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why is meticulous skin antisepsis necessary when drawing blood cultures?

options.A: To prevent skin contaminants from causing false-positive results
options.B: To ensure the blood clots faster in the vial
options.C: To destroy all red blood cells in the sample
options.D: To speed up the transportation process

explanation: Proper skin antisepsis prevents skin contaminants, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, from contaminating the sample and causing false-positive results. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h5)

question: What type of immunity develops following exposure to an antigen or through vaccination?
explanation: Adaptive immunity is acquired immunity that develops after exposure to an antigen or through vaccination, generating specific antibodies and memory cells. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the purpose of herd immunity in a community?

options.A: To eliminate the need for proper hand hygiene
options.B: To protect vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated
options.C: To ensure every individual gets infected simultaneously
options.D: To replace the cold-chain storage system

explanation: High vaccination rates create herd immunity, protecting vulnerable individuals who are unable to receive vaccines themselves. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why do wounds represent a significant risk for infection in patients?

options.A: They enhance the body's natural immune barriers
options.B: They compromise the skin's barrier, creating a portal of entry for pathogens
options.C: They prevent any microorganisms from multiplying
options.D: They eliminate the need for antimicrobial therapy

explanation: Wounds compromise the protective skin barrier, creating a direct portal of entry for environmental and commensal pathogens to cause infection. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the difference between a bactericidal and a bacteriostatic agent?

options.A: Bactericidal kills bacteria, while bacteriostatic inhibits their growth
options.B: Bactericidal inhibits growth, while bacteriostatic kills bacteria
options.C: Bactericidal only works on viruses, while bacteriostatic works on fungi
options.D: There is no functional difference between the two terms

explanation: Bactericidal agents directly kill bacteria, whereas bacteriostatic agents inhibit bacterial replication and growth, relying on the host immune system to clear the rest. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h7)
